result:
The proposed answer of 1/8 is incorrect. The correct limit is **1/10**.

**Structure of the graph.** Identify each vertex $\{i,j\}$ with the lattice point $(i,j)$, where $1 \le i < j \le n$. Moving a token changes one coordinate by $\pm 1$, and the move is allowed only if the new coordinates stay in the region $i<j$. So $T_2(P_n)$ is an induced subgraph of the square grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$, with no diagonal edges, on a staircase triangle of $N = \binom{n}{2} \sim n^2/2$ vertices.

**Lower bound.** Every vertex of the grid has degree at most 4, so its closed neighbourhood has at most 5 vertices. A dominating set $D$ must therefore satisfy $5|D| \ge N$, giving $\gamma \ge N/5 \sim n^2/10$.

**Upper bound.** The infinite grid has a perfect dominating pattern of density $1/5$. Restricting that pattern to the triangle gives a dominating set of size about $N/5$, plus $O(n)$ extra vertices to dominate the boundary vertices that the pattern misses. Boundary terms are $O(n)$, which is negligible against $n^2$, so $\gamma \sim N/5 \sim n^2/10$.

Hence $\gamma(T_2(P_n))/n^2 \to 1/10$.

**Problems with the proposed solution.**
- It correctly notes the $1/5$ grid density and the vertex count $\sim n^2/2$, which together already give $1/10$.
- It then discards this reasoning and asserts that boundary effects change the density. Boundary effects are only $O(n)$ and cannot change the leading term.
- The claimed sequence "observed in several studies" is not supported by any citation, and the stated values do not establish a $n^2/8$ law. A $1/8$ density would also exceed the trivial lower bound $1/10$ only by a factor the boundary cannot produce, so the claim is inconsistent with the structure of the graph.

VERDICT: REJECT
